issues.legal_issue: A family arrangement may be inferred from a long course of separate possession and dealings asserting exclusive ownership.
material_facts: The family members took separate possession of different properties after the division attributed to the family matriarch.
Over many years, the daughters and grandsons separately mortgaged, sold, and otherwise dealt with the properties as absolute owners.
The family members’ asserted sources of title varied, but their repeated assertions of separate and exclusive ownership were consistent.
The plaintiff had himself asserted absolute ownership over properties allocated to him and had represented the family arrangement to a lender.
issues.conclusion: The course of conduct established that a family arrangement had been made, under which the matriarch claimed the whole estate and the family members accepted separate absolute estates in allotted portions.
issues.legal_principle: A family arrangement may be inferred from a long course of dealings between family members: Clifton v. Cockburn, [1834] 3 My. & K. 76; William v. William, [1866] L.R. 2 Ch. 294. The Court considered the family’s possession, transactions, admissions, and statements as evidence of the arrangement, and held that the varying explanations of the source of title did not defeat the inference where the separate claims of absolute ownership were consistent.

rule.if: family_property_title_dispute and long_separate_possession and repeated_separate_dealings and members_asserted_absolute_ownership

predicates.family_property_title_dispute: Family members disputed whether properties were held under separate absolute titles or under an earlier family estate.
predicates.long_separate_possession: Different family members held separate portions of the properties over a long period.
predicates.repeated_separate_dealings: Family members repeatedly mortgaged, sold, or otherwise dealt with their allotted properties separately.
predicates.members_asserted_absolute_ownership: Family members asserted that they exclusively owned the properties they separately possessed.

issues.definition: When family members in a property-title dispute possess separate portions and repeatedly deal with them while asserting exclusive ownership, their conduct can establish a family arrangement.

issues.legal_issue: A family arrangement may recognize one member’s claim to the whole property and provide for the transfer of allotted portions to other members, subject to the transfer formalities applicable when the arrangement was made.
material_facts: The matriarch had asserted an absolute claim to the properties, while the daughters and grandsons later claimed separate absolute ownership of allotted portions.
The daughters accepted the division and received allotted properties; the grandsons received separate properties while they were minors.
The arrangement was made orally in 1875, when the applicable law did not require a writing for the transfer and the later registration requirement did not apply in the absence of a writing.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the arrangement as sufficient to pass title: the daughters’ allotted interests arose under the family arrangement, and the oral arrangement was sufficient for the transfers made in 1875.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, a family arrangement acknowledges and defines antecedent titles, with each participant giving up claims to property allotted to others; no conveyance is then needed because the arrangement recognizes the title as already residing in the recipient. The Court extended the principle, in the absence of fraud, to an arrangement in which members relinquish claims and accept gifts or transfers from the family member asserting the whole title. In that situation, transfer formalities must be observed; here, the arrangement predated the Transfer of Property Act and no writing was required, so the Registration Act did not apply. The Court referred to and distinguished Rani Mewa Kuwar v. Rani Hulas Kuwar, [1874] 1 I.A. 157; Khunni Lal v. Gobind Krishna Narain, [1911] 38 I.A. 87; and Ramsumran Prasad v. Shyam Kumari, [1922] 49 I.A. 348.

rule.if: family_arrangement_in_property_dispute and one_member_claimed_whole_title and other_members_accepted_allocated_properties and arrangement_was_oral and applicable_law_required_no_writing

predicates.family_arrangement_in_property_dispute: Family members settled competing claims to property through an arrangement allocating separate portions.
predicates.one_member_claimed_whole_title: One family member asserted ownership of the whole property before making allocations to other members.
predicates.other_members_accepted_allocated_propert: Other family members accepted the properties allotted to them in return for giving up claims to other portions.
predicates.arrangement_was_oral: The family members made the arrangement orally rather than in a written instrument.
predicates.applicable_law_required_no_writing: The law applicable when the arrangement was made did not require a writing to transfer the property.

issues.definition: An oral arrangement can transfer title when one family member claims the whole property, the others accept their allotted portions, and the applicable law did not require a writing.

issues.legal_issue: A reversioner who knowingly and unequivocally assents to a transaction that is voidable at his instance may be precluded from later avoiding it, even if he assented before becoming entitled to the estate.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s interest as reversioner became operative only after the limited estates ended.
Before then, he expressly assented to the absolute titles of other family members and engaged in a long course of dealings asserting absolute titles himself.
The plaintiff represented the arrangement to a lender, demonstrating knowledge of its nature, and accepted benefits under the arrangement.
The Court found that the plaintiff’s assent was to the family arrangement as a whole, rather than only to an individual gift.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff, having knowingly and unequivocally assented to the arrangement and accepted benefits under it, was precluded from avoiding it after the succession opened.
issues.legal_principle: An alienation by a widow beyond her powers is voidable by the reversioner, not void; a reversioner may be precluded from avoiding it by ratification or conduct treating it as binding. A person who, with full knowledge of his rights, elects to assent to a voidable transaction cannot later reverse that election. Assent may be given before the reversioner becomes entitled to sue, and may be inferred from conduct amounting to an actual election, but must clearly relate to the transaction in question. The Court relied on Raja Modhu Sudan Singh v. Rooke, [1897] 24 I.A. 164; Bijoy Gopal v. Krishna, [1906] 34 I.A. 87; Ramgouda Annagowda v. Bhausaheb, [1927] 54 I.A. 396; Rangaswami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, [1918] 46 I.A. 72; and Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, 1952 S.C.R. 478.

rule.if: reversioner_challenges_voidable_transaction and reversioner_knew_material_facts and reversioner_unequivocally_assented and assent_related_to_whole_transaction and reversioner_accepted_benefit

predicates.reversioner_challenges_voidable_transact: A person who has become entitled as reversioner seeks to avoid a transaction affecting the estate.
predicates.reversioner_knew_material_facts: The reversioner knew the material facts about the transaction and the rights he could assert against it.
predicates.reversioner_unequivocally_assented: The reversioner clearly acted in a way showing assent to the transaction.
predicates.assent_related_to_whole_transaction: The reversioner’s assent concerned the overall transaction rather than only a separate disposition within it.
predicates.reversioner_accepted_benefit: The reversioner received or accepted a benefit under the transaction.

issues.definition: A reversioner who knows the material facts, clearly assents to the whole transaction, and accepts a benefit cannot later avoid that transaction after becoming entitled to do so.

issues.legal_issue: A person may be personally estopped from challenging a transfer when he represented the asserted title to a purchaser before the purchaser acquired the property.
material_facts: Before the first defendant acquired the disputed properties, the plaintiff and his brother represented to him that family members held absolute titles under the family arrangement.
The first defendant later acquired the properties through a subsequent sale and, as to another property, through pre-emption.
issues.conclusion: In the appeal involving those later acquisitions, the Court held that the plaintiff was also personally estopped from challenging the transfers, although it relied on the reversioner’s election as sufficient to dispose of both appeals.
issues.legal_principle: A party’s representation concerning title may prevent that party from denying the represented position against a person who acquired property after the representation. The Court stated that the additional estoppel in this appeal was governed by Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, 1952 S.C.R. 478, but did not elaborate because the separate principle of election was sufficient to decide the appeals.

predicates.property_transfer_challenge: A claimant seeks to challenge a transfer of property.
predicates.claimant_represented_absolute_title_to_p: Before the acquisition, the claimant represented to the eventual purchaser that the relevant family members held absolute title.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_property_after_repres: The purchaser acquired the property after the claimant made the representation.

issues.definition: A claimant who represents absolute title to a purchaser before the purchaser acquires the property may be prevented from later challenging the transfer.
